name: Fred Fine
bio: Fred Fine was a Communist Party leader indicted under the Smith Act in 1951 who went underground as a 'Smith Act refugee' rather than stand trial. He surrendered voluntarily in December 1955, was held on $20,000 bail, and faced trial in February 1956.
charges: Smith Act — conspiracy to advocate the overthrow of the government
convicted: Indicted 1951; a fugitive until surrendering December 1955

name: James E. Jackson
bio: James E. Jackson Jr. was a Black Communist Party leader from the South, indicted under the Smith Act in 1951, who went underground as a 'Smith Act refugee.' He surrendered voluntarily in December 1955, saying his surrender would 'further serve the popular fight to restore the Bill of Rights,' and was held on $20,000 bail.
charges: Smith Act — conspiracy to advocate the overthrow of the government
convicted: Indicted 1951; a fugitive until surrendering December 1955

name: William Norman
bio: William Norman was a Communist Party figure indicted under the Smith Act in 1951 with Fred Fine and James Jackson. He surrendered in Newark, New Jersey in December 1955 and was held on $20,000 bail.
charges: Smith Act — conspiracy to advocate the overthrow of the government

name: Sidney Steinberg
bio: Sidney Steinberg was a Communist Party member who was jailed for 'harboring' the fugitive Smith Act leader Robert Thompson and was himself among those indicted under the Smith Act in the 1951 New York case. He was arrested early in 1955 and set for the fall 1955 Smith Act trial.
charges: Harboring a Smith Act fugitive; and Smith Act conspiracy
convicted: Jailed for harboring; arrested 1955 for the Smith Act trial
sentence: Serving a term for harboring; facing the Smith Act trial

name: John Noto
bio: John Noto was a Buffalo Communist Party leader arrested on August 31, 1955 under a 1954 sealed indictment charging membership in the Communist Party under the Smith Act. He was jailed on bail set at $30,000 cash; his case, Noto v. United States, later reached the Supreme Court.
convicted: Arrested August 1955 under a sealed indictment

name: Max Weiss
bio: Max Weiss was a Communist Party leader, formerly of Chicago, arrested in New York City on September 19, 1955 under a sealed 1954 Smith Act indictment, even though he had been living openly with his family for years. The FBI had planted stories that he had gone underground.
convicted: Arrested September 1955 under a sealed indictment

name: Alfred Marder
bio: Alfred Marder, a New Haven printer, was one of the Connecticut Communists indicted in the New Haven Smith Act case. After the first indictment was dismissed for an improperly drawn jury in February 1955, the group was re-indicted on March 4, 1955; the convictions were later reversed by the Second Circuit in United States v. Silverman (1957).
charges: Smith Act — conspiracy to advocate the overthrow of the government
convicted: Indicted 1954; re-indicted March 1955; conviction reversed on appeal
sentence: Convicted under the Smith Act; reversed in United States v. Silverman

name: Sidney Resnek
bio: Sidney Resnek, a Connecticut printer, was one of the New Haven Smith Act defendants. After the original indictment was thrown out for an improperly drawn jury in February 1955, he and his co-defendants were re-indicted on March 4, 1955; the convictions were later reversed by the Second Circuit in United States v. Silverman (1957).
charges: Smith Act — conspiracy to advocate the overthrow of the government
convicted: Indicted 1954; re-indicted March 1955; conviction reversed on appeal
sentence: Convicted under the Smith Act; reversed in United States v. Silverman

name: James Tate
bio: James Tate, a Connecticut sidewalk contractor, was one of the New Haven Smith Act defendants re-indicted on March 4, 1955 after the original indictment was dismissed over an improperly drawn jury. The group's convictions were later reversed by the Second Circuit in United States v. Silverman (1957).
charges: Smith Act — conspiracy to advocate the overthrow of the government
convicted: Indicted 1954; re-indicted March 1955; conviction reversed on appeal
sentence: Convicted under the Smith Act; reversed in United States v. Silverman

name: Pablo Garcia
bio: Pablo Garcia Rodriguez was a Harvard-trained civil-rights lawyer and member of the central committee of the Communist Party of Puerto Rico, arrested October 20, 1954 in the first Smith Act prosecution ever brought in Puerto Rico. He was one of eleven defendants awaiting trial in San Juan in an English-language proceeding their lawyers said they could not understand.
charges: Smith Act — conspiracy to advocate the overthrow of the government
convicted: Arrested October 1954; awaiting trial in Puerto Rico
sentence: Faced a mainland prison term if convicted

name: Juan Santos Rivera
bio: Juan Santos Rivera was the president of the Communist Party of Puerto Rico, arrested in October 1954 in the first Smith Act case brought on the island. He was one of eleven defendants awaiting trial in San Juan; speaking no English, he protested he could not confront his accusers in an English-language trial.
charges: Smith Act — conspiracy to advocate the overthrow of the government
convicted: Arrested October 1954; awaiting trial in Puerto Rico
sentence: Faced a mainland prison term if convicted

name: Ramon Mirabal
bio: Ramon Mirabal was the secretary-general of the Communist Party of Puerto Rico, arrested in October 1954 in the island's first Smith Act prosecution. He was one of eleven defendants awaiting trial in San Juan and, speaking no English, faced the prospect of a trial he could not follow.
charges: Smith Act — conspiracy to advocate the overthrow of the government
convicted: Arrested October 1954; awaiting trial in Puerto Rico
sentence: Faced a mainland prison term if convicted

name: William Allan
bio: William Allan was a Detroit Communist and labor writer for the Michigan Worker, convicted of conspiracy under the Smith Act. In 1955 the government additionally moved to strip his citizenship through denaturalization proceedings, hoping to use his case to overturn the 1943 Schneiderman precedent.
charges: Smith Act — conspiracy; then denaturalization proceedings
convicted: Convicted under the Smith Act; targeted for denaturalization (1955)

name: William Schneiderman
bio: William Schneiderman was a California Communist Party leader convicted of conspiracy under the Smith Act. He had earlier been the subject of the 1943 Supreme Court case Schneiderman v. United States, in which Wendell Willkie successfully defended his citizenship against a denaturalization attempt.
charges: Smith Act — conspiracy to advocate the overthrow of the government

name: Philip M. Connelly
bio: Philip M. Connelly was a California Communist journalist and former state CIO leader, one of the fourteen California Communists convicted in the 1952 Los Angeles Smith Act trial. His conviction was on appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court, which in 1957 reversed the California convictions in Yates v. United States.
charges: Smith Act — conspiracy to advocate the overthrow of the government
convicted: Convicted 1952; on appeal to the Supreme Court
sentence: Up to five years and a $10,000 fine; on bail pending appeal

name: William J. Pennock
bio: William J. Pennock was the long-time president of the Washington Pension Union and a defendant in the 1953 Seattle Smith Act trial, a prosecution that was part of the government's drive against the union. He died while the trial was still in progress.
charges: Smith Act — conspiracy to advocate the overthrow of the government
convicted: On trial (Seattle, 1953); died during the trial
